scenario: Reaching the flawed monitoring function requires an already provisioned ordinary account, limited to the user’s own settings; the attacker cannot self-register or otherwise grant themselves that account. The attacker acts alone. A separately functioning analytics service with independent security policies is the only other affected system. The attacker already could read every analytics record before the exploit and obtains no additional information or modification rights. Successful exploitation completely denies legitimate users access to analytics for as long as the attacker continues invoking the flaw.

The investigator happens to possess an administrator account for a routing service. The report does not establish whether the flawed endpoint requires any account or privileges, or can be reached without authentication. The investigator triggers the flaw with no other human action. It causes a separately functioning scheduling service with its own security policies to change one cosmetic display label without authorization; no other data can be changed, and this modification has no direct serious consequence. Scheduling availability is unchanged. The report does not establish whether any restricted scheduling information can become visible through the flaw. No other systems are affected.
